title: Jury in coroner's inquest hears how woman from Alberta died in northwestern Ontario

blocks.text: Thunder Bay·In-Depth

The first day of a coroner's inquest into the death of a woman at Lake of the Woods District Hospital in Kenora, Ont., took place via video conference on Monday. Here's what members of the jury heard about the late Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild of Tsuut’ina Nation in southern Alberta and how she ended up in northwestern Ontario.
Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild of Tsuut’ina Nation died on Sept. 20, 2022
WARNING: This story contains references to sexual assault and suicide. Resources can be found at the bottom of this story.
Michelle Crowchild says her daughter, Kaylee Martha Dallas Crowchild, was a kind and loving person who would give her last dollar to someone in need.
A coroner’s inquest into Kaylee’s death began on Monday. The 29-year-old was a member of Tsuut’ina Nation, a Dene community about 40 kilometres southwest of Calgary, Alberta.
The jury heard that Kaylee died on Sept. 20, 2022 at Lake of the Woods District Hospital in Kenora, Ont., after being transferred from the Kenora District Jail.
Inquests are mandatory under the Coroners Act when a person dies in custody. The proceedings are being held via video conference.

In a coroner’s inquest, witnesses provide information about the circumstances surrounding a person’s death, after which a five-person jury is tasked with identifying who died, when and where the person died, their medical cause of death and means of death.

Jurors will then classify how the death happened: due to natural causes, accident, homicide, suicide or undetermined. While they cannot make any legal findings or lay blame on anyone, they may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
The Kenora District Jail in northwestern Ontario is seen in this screenshot from Google Maps. (Google Streetview)

On Monday, the jury heard that Kaylee’s inquest is expected to focus on suicide screening within the Kenora District Jail, policies in place in 2022 during the COVID-19 pandemic, and cultural supports for Indigenous inmates.

Between 2023-2024, more than 30 per cent of adult inmates at provincial and federal correctional facilities were Indigenous, despite the fact that Indigenous people comprised only four per cent of Canada’s population at this time, according to Statistics Canada.
She was a daughter, a mother, family member, friend and community member whose life encompassed experiences beyond the events that brought us here today.Makenzie Chan, inquest counsel

“While this data is important to acknowledge, it is equally important to remember that Miss Crowchild is more than the circumstances in which she found herself in at the Kenora Jail,” said Makenzie Chan, who is serving as inquest counsel alongside Robert Kozak and Jenna Simpson.
“She was a daughter, a mother, family member, friend and community member whose life encompassed experiences beyond the events that brought us here today.”
Mother asks jury to think of her 'as a person'
Jurors heard that Kaylee was one of seven siblings. She loved dancing and music, especially the Spice Girls, and enjoyed cooking, cleaning and helping her mother, Michelle Crowchild said.
The jury heard of Kaylee’s struggles in her youth. She was sexually assaulted by a family member at a young age, something her mother only found out after her death.
Residents of Black Bear Crossing in Tsuut’ina Nation were forced to evacuate in 2006 due to asbestos and other health concerns at the former military barracks. (CBC)

In 2006 when she was 13 years old, her family was forced to evacuate from their home at Black Bear Crossing in Tsuut’ina Nation and leave all their belongings behind. The former military barracks was deemed uninhabitable due to asbestos and other health concerns.
During the eight months her family lived in a hotel, Kaylee kept running away, her mother said. Around this time, she started using alcohol and drugs, and eventually ended up living on the streets.
In the days leading up to her death, Kaylee ended up in hospital in Brandon, Man. Her mother was told she refused treatment and was seen leaving with two men.
On Sept. 14, 2022, she was arrested in Dryden, Ont. She told police she was sexually assaulted the day before, the jury heard.
Michelle Crowchild says Kaylee had never left Alberta before this point. Her family believes she may have been the victim of human trafficking.
Kaylee was eligible for release from jail the day after her arrest but needed $100 in bail money, the jury heard.

blocks.text: Her mother was told she died by suicide six days after being taken into custody.
“I still don't want to believe that,” Michelle Crowchild said. “She loved her children too much. She loved her family too much.”
Kaylee leaves behind a 10-year-old son, who is being raised by her mother, and a six-year-old daughter who has been placed in care.

blocks.text: Michelle Crowchild told the jury she hopes they think of her daughter as a person and not just as someone who was dealing with addiction.
“She was a mom, she was a young girl and she was a member of our community and loved dearly,” she said.
The inquest is expected to last six days and hear from about 11 witnesses. People can watch a livestream of the proceedings online here.
